content: Routine vaccines are those that are recommended for all individuals in the United States based on their age and vaccination history. These vaccines are often associated with childhood immunizations administered before starting school, but there are also routine vaccines specifically recommended for adolescents and adults. Routine vaccines are particularly important for travelers. In the United States, many vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles, mumps, and chickenpox, are uncommon due to widespread vaccination. However, if you are not vaccinated, traveling internationally increases your risk of contracting and spreading diseases that are rare in the U.S. but still prevalent in other parts of the world. For example, popular travel destinations, including Europe, continue to experience outbreaks of measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. Ensuring that you are up-to-date on all routine vaccines is essential to protect yourself from infectious diseases like measles, which can spread rapidly among unvaccinated individuals. Many diseases that are uncommon in the United States due to routine vaccination remain widespread in other countries. Before traveling, it is important to check the CDC’s destination-specific health information to determine which vaccines or medications you may need and to understand the health risks associated with your destination. It is recommended to schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider or a travel health specialist at least one month before your departure. During this consultation, your provider can administer destination-specific vaccines, prescribe necessary medications, and provide tailored advice based on your health status, travel itinerary, and planned activities. The specific routine vaccines you may need before traveling depend on factors such as your age, health condition, and vaccination history. In some cases, you may require an accelerated vaccine schedule or a booster dose prior to travel. Routine vaccines that may be relevant for travelers include: Chickenpox (Varicella) Hepatitis A Hepatitis B Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis (Tdap) Shingles (Zoster) The CDC provides detailed immunization schedules based on age groups, which include:
